task.goal: Help first-time library volunteers handle a disagreement about a shared room booking without taking sides prematurely.
hard_constraints: A 45-minute training with role cards and one facilitator.
Do not ask trainees to recount personal conflicts; no legal or disciplinary advice.
Practice must include verifying the booking record, listening to both parties, and knowing when to escalate; assess an unseen scenario individually.
task.available_resources: Fictional booking records and policy excerpt.
task.expected_result: A role-play sequence and actionable escalation check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A three-gate conversation protocol
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give novices three gates—hear both accounts, verify the record, then resolve or escalate. Requiring observable evidence before a decision could reduce premature siding, although trainees may follow the sequence mechanically.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce neutrality and the fictional policy; 5–10 the facilitator demonstrates the gates; 10–28 run three six-minute role-play rounds in triads, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–35 discuss missed gates and repeat difficult moments; 35–43 complete an unseen individual scenario; 43–45 review the escalation check. Nobody recounts personal conflicts.

Role cards give each room user a plausible claim, one relevant detail, and an immediate need. The volunteer receives the booking record and policy excerpt. Each round includes listening to both parties, summarizing each account without endorsing it, checking room/date/time/status in the record, explaining what is established, and proposing only policy-supported next steps.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern? Follow the excerpt’s safety route. Is the record missing, contradictory, or insufficient? Pause allocation and contact the designated staff member. Does the requested exception exceed volunteer authority, or does disagreement persist after clarification? Escalate with both accounts, verified facts, unresolved questions, and the next update time. Avoid blame, sanctions, and legal conclusions.

Needs: one facilitator, printed role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt specifying volunteer authority and a staff contact route. Assume enough trainees for triads; a pair can alternate the second claimant role. The protocol cannot settle ambiguities the policy leaves unresolved.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two matched unseen written scenarios, counterbalanced across trainees: one answered before instruction using ordinary judgment, one afterward using the gates. Score record verification, fair hearing, and justified escalation separately. A minimal falsifying result is that protocol users still allocate the room before hearing both claims, or escalate clear routine cases without justification. This small comparison checks usability and immediate performance, not lasting transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An evidence-gap role-play
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distribute incomplete but compatible information across the two claimants and the booking record. The volunteer can reach a defensible next step only by asking both parties questions and cross-checking the record. This makes impartial listening useful for solving the task, rather than merely a courtesy.

Allocate 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–9 demonstrate separating a claim from a verified fact; 9–27 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating roles; 27–34 reveal the evidence and discuss unsupported assumptions; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation handoffs. Use fictional situations exclusively.

Each claimant card states what to disclose initially and what to disclose when asked. For example, one person has a confirmation for a different room; the other has the correct room but an outdated time. The booking record establishes current status. Later rounds include a genuinely unresolved discrepancy so that finding more information does not always produce a volunteer-level resolution. Volunteers must hear both accounts and inspect the record in every round.

The escalation check asks: Can I establish the booking from the available record? Does the policy authorize my proposed next step? Can the interaction continue safely and constructively? If any answer is no, use the excerpt’s designated staff route. State what each person reports, what the record confirms, what remains uncertain, and what assistance is needed. Do not assign fault or invent consequences.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and records, and a policy excerpt defining authority and escalation contacts. Card preparation requires care: avoid trick wording and ensure information becomes available through reasonable questions. Limits include reading demands and trainees learning to hunt for hidden clues rather than listen naturally.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one ordinary full-information practice case with one evidence-gap case, counterbalancing order. Then give everyone the same unseen individual case with both accounts and a record available. Check whether trainees identify the decisive discrepancy, acknowledge both accounts, and choose a supported action. The mechanism is weakened if evidence-gap practice produces more guessing or clue-hunting without better verification than ordinary practice.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Pause, compare, and replay decision points
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: rehearse the moment when a volunteer is tempted to decide too early. Short pauses let trainees compare a premature response with an evidence-seeking response, then immediately replay the conversation. The intended change is recognition of decision hazards under pressure; improvement is uncertain until tested without pauses.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and respectful boundaries; 5–10 the facilitator models a rushed decision and invites a replacement line; 10–28 triads complete three six-minute rounds, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 28–34 review decision points; 34–42 complete an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 review the escalation check. All examples are fictional, with no requests for personal experiences.

Role cards introduce distinct pressures: an apparently confident claimant, an urgent request, or two conflicting confirmations. Every round requires listening to both parties and inspecting the booking record. A printed pause marker appears after the opening claims and after record inspection. At each marker the volunteer states what is known, what remains unverified, and the next question or action. The triad briefly compares two responses, selects the policy-supported response, and replays from the marker. The facilitator circulates and corrects substantive misunderstandings.

Actionable escalation check: stop and use the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; seek designated staff when records conflict, authority is insufficient, or disagreement persists after a clear explanation. Give a neutral handoff containing both accounts, verified booking details, the unresolved issue, and the requested staff decision. Avoid disciplinary or legal advice.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards with pause markers, fictional records, and an excerpt defining escalation routes. Assume trainees can use the markers without constant facilitator supervision. Pauses may make practice easier than real service, so the final assessment removes them.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Have trainees first answer a brief unseen case without prompts, then assess a matched unseen case individually after rehearsal. Require their opening response, record checks, summaries of both accounts, and escalation decision. Compare against the simple pretraining response. A falsifying signal is successful prompted replay followed by premature siding or unsupported decisions when markers disappear; that would suggest dependence on rehearsal cues rather than transferable judgment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reverse the claimants, preserve the facts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: replay the same dispute after swapping the claimants’ presentation styles while preserving every booking fact. A confident, familiar-sounding claimant becomes hesitant; the other becomes assertive. Comparing the volunteer’s responses makes reliance on confidence or apparent familiarity visible. The intended change is a more stable judgment based on verified facts and both accounts, rather than personal impressions. This differs from simply rotating practice roles: the controlled reversal is the teaching device.

Use 45 minutes: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–10 explain role cards and neutral opening language; 10–28 run three six-minute triad cycles, rotating the volunteer. Each cycle includes a short encounter, a replay with claimant styles reversed, and comparison. Use 28–33 to discuss which responses changed and why; 33–42 for an unseen individual assessment; 42–45 for the escalation check. Use fictional disputes only; offer no legal or disciplinary advice.

Both versions require the volunteer to hear each party, summarize their accounts, and verify room, date, time, and booking status against the record. Cards specify identical substantive information across versions, disclosed without requiring clever questions. Respectful listening should remain consistent even when delivery changes.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate danger; contact designated staff if records remain contradictory, a requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement persists after explanation. Hand over both accounts, verified details, the unresolved question, and the assistance needed.

Needs: one facilitator, paired role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Triads must manage timing independently. Style changes should avoid identity stereotypes. Repetition may itself improve performance, and trainees may recognize the lesson without transferring it to service.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads a style-reversal replay and others an identical replay, with equal practice time. Everyone then answers the same unseen scenario individually, stating their opening response, questions for both parties, record checks, and escalation decision. Compare premature allocation and unsupported reliance on confidence. The mechanism is weakened if reversal practice produces no improvement over ordinary repetition, or merely makes trainees favor the quieter claimant. This checks immediate transfer, not durable behavior.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Learn the boundary through contrasting cases
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish cases they can handle from cases requiring staff by comparing closely matched disputes whose decisive difference is authority or evidence quality. Contrast can expose the actual escalation boundary: a clear record supports one action, while an unresolved discrepancy or unauthorized exception requires staff. This aims to prevent both premature decisions and automatic escalation of every disagreement.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–11 compare two short case files differing in one decisive fact; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 29–34 compare decisions against the excerpt; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 rehearse a staff handoff. All situations are fictional; do not solicit personal conflicts or provide legal or disciplinary advice.

Prepare three practice packets: a routine case with a clear current booking, a matched case with conflicting current records, and a clear booking accompanied by an exception request outside volunteer authority. Role cards give both claimants reasonable concerns. In every encounter, volunteers listen to both parties and verify room, date, time, and status before choosing a next step. Trainees explain which specific fact or policy provision permits action or requires escalation; politeness alone does not count as a justified decision.

Actionable escalation check: Is there an immediate safety concern requiring the excerpt’s safety route? Can the booking be established? Is the proposed action within volunteer authority? Does disagreement persist after clarification? For unresolved evidence, insufficient authority, or persistent disagreement, contact designated staff and report both accounts, confirmed details, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, coordinated role cards and fictional records, and a policy excerpt with explicit authority boundaries and contacts. Assume triads can run from printed directions. Contrasts must be realistic and unambiguous; overly tidy examples could teach brittle rules that fail on mixed cases.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot contrasting-case instruction against an equal-length explanation using unrelated examples, keeping role-play time equal. Give each trainee one unseen case combining a clear booking with an unauthorized exception request. Individually assess whether they hear both accounts, verify the record, and distinguish confirmed booking facts from the staff decision required. A falsifying result is equally frequent unsupported allocation or blanket escalation without identifying the authority boundary. A single small pilot offers only preliminary evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build a shared account before proposing action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a visible, three-column worksheet—“Party A reports,” “Party B reports,” and “Record confirms”—to keep claims separate from established facts. Before proposing action, the volunteer reads back the account and invites each claimant to correct their own entry. Externalizing the information could reduce memory errors and make accidental endorsement visible. Agreement about who should use the room is not required.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate the worksheet; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating volunteer and two room users; 28–34 review worksheets and practice neutral corrections; 34–42 assess an unseen scenario individually; 42–45 review escalation. Discuss fictional cases only; solicit no personal conflicts and give no legal or disciplinary advice.

Role cards give each claimant a booking claim and a practical concern. The volunteer hears both accounts, records them without treating either as verified, and checks room, date, time, and status against the fictional record. Each claimant checks their own summary. Corrections remain attributed unless independently confirmed. The volunteer then explains which next step the policy supports.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns. Contact designated staff when booking evidence remains unresolved, the requested action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement continues after clarification. Hand over both accounts, verified details, remaining uncertainty, and the assistance needed. Never treat a claimant’s refusal to endorse the worksheet as proof against them.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, a policy excerpt specifying authority and contacts, and blank worksheets. Assume a manageable group working in self-directed triads. Writing may slow conversation; concise notes and reading entries aloud reduce that burden. The worksheet cannot establish whether the underlying record is accurate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In a small pilot, give some triads the worksheet and others ordinary blank paper, with identical instructions and practice time. Assess everyone individually on the same unseen packet containing two accounts and a booking record. Score whether they distinguish claims from verified facts, represent both parties accurately, and justify action or escalation. The mechanism is weakened if worksheets produce equally frequent claim-as-fact errors, or accurate notes followed by unsupported allocation. This checks immediate performance, not durable transfer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Practice repairing a premature commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach a specific recovery skill for when a volunteer has already appeared to take sides. Rehearsing an explicit correction may make it easier to withdraw an unsupported commitment instead of defending it. The intended outcome is recoverable judgment: a novice notices the mistake, acknowledges it, and resumes fair inquiry. Whether that transfers beyond rehearsal remains uncertain.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 explain the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 demonstrate a repair; 10–28 complete three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 discuss repair language and repeat weak attempts; 34–42 assess an unseen case individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Use fictional material exclusively, without personal-conflict disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice.

Each round begins with a printed statement attributed to the volunteer, such as “I said you could have the room before checking the booking.” Trainees do not need to invent or perform the initial mistake. Their task is to repair it: “I spoke before checking the information. I need to hear both accounts and verify the booking before explaining the next step.” They then listen to both claimants, summarize each account, and inspect room, date, time, and booking status. Role cards let a claimant ask whether the earlier promise still stands. The volunteer must explain the correction without blaming either person or promising an unauthorized remedy.

Escalation check: follow the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved records, requests beyond volunteer authority, or continuing disagreement after clarification. Include the earlier commitment in the handoff alongside both accounts, verified facts, and the decision needed.

Needs: one facilitator, role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt defining authority and staff contacts. Assume triads can follow printed timing. Model the correction prominently so trainees do not mistake the opening error for acceptable practice. Repair must not become a substitute for careful initial handling.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare recovery rehearsal with equal-time practice that begins before any commitment, using the same policy and verification requirements. Give each trainee an unseen individual scenario in which a volunteer’s earlier assurance conflicts with newly available information. Ask for their next words, checks, and escalation decision. Recovery practice is not supported if trainees preserve the unsupported promise, blame a claimant, or retract it without hearing both parties and checking the record. Include a fresh-start item to inspect whether rehearsing mistakes inadvertently normalizes premature commitments.

EXPAND.title: Calibrate the boundary between acting and handing off
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach volunteers to distinguish a routine booking correction from a decision requiring staff authority through closely matched cases. This targets unnecessary escalation as well as unsupported independent action. The learning comes from contrasting the fact that changes the authorized response, rather than memorizing a conversation sequence.

Preparation: the facilitator creates role cards, records, and a fictional policy excerpt defining routine volunteer actions, staff-only exceptions, and contact routes. A close pair differs in one consequential detail: in one case a claimant’s confirmation concerns another room and the current record is unambiguous; in the other, two current confirmations conflict. An unfamiliar case concerns a request to override a clearly valid booking.

Run 45 minutes: 0–6 explain authority and model respectful listening; 6–12 trainees individually choose actions for the close pair, then discuss the decisive difference; 12–30 run three six-minute triad role-plays with rotating volunteers; 30–34 review choices and consequences; 34–43 assess an unseen close pair and unfamiliar case individually; 43–45 review the handoff.

Every role-play requires hearing and neutrally summarizing both accounts, checking room, date, time, and status in the record, and explaining the policy-supported next step. Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; contradictory or insufficient records, an unauthorized exception, or continuing disagreement after clarification—contact designated staff. Otherwise carry out the authorized routine action. Give staff both accounts, verified facts, the unresolved decision, and the requested help. Tell both users how an update will arrive; if staff are unavailable, follow the excerpt’s fallback without promising allocation.

Needs: one facilitator and printed fictional materials; assume triads. Use no personal conflict accounts or legal or disciplinary advice. The main limitation is dependence on a policy excerpt that actually defines authority clearly.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator owns a first trial across two small training groups: compare this session with an equal-length three-gate session using identical individual assessment cases. Score appropriate routine action, justified escalation, both-party listening, and record verification. Also count unnecessary staff referrals and preparation time. Stop using the contrast exercise if trainees learn superficial case cues, miss a required handoff, or show no better boundary decisions while adding referrals or preparation burden. This tests immediate judgment only; a small trial cannot establish durable transfer.

EXPAND.title: Test neutrality by exchanging claimant identities
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make premature siding visible through an identity-swap test. Trainees encounter the same booking evidence with the claimants’ confidence, familiarity with the library, and stated urgency exchanged. A decision that changes without a relevant change in evidence exposes an unreliable basis for allocating the room.

Preparation: produce three paired sets of role cards with identical underlying booking facts. In the first version, the confident regular has the valid booking; in its counterpart, the hesitant newcomer does. Keep policy-relevant facts constant within each pair and avoid demographic stereotypes. The policy states that confidence, familiarity, and unsupported urgency do not establish booking priority.

Use 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the policy and fictional-only boundaries; 5–10 trainees privately judge two short identity-swapped openings, then identify evidence still needed; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds, rotating the volunteer. Each volunteer hears both accounts, verifies the booking record, explains the supported action, and completes any handoff. At each round’s end, reveal the swapped counterpart and ask whether the decision should change and why. Use 28–34 to discuss evidence-based reasons for changing a decision; 34–43 for an unseen individual written scenario without swap prompts; 43–45 for the escalation check.

Escalation check: follow the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; contact designated staff for unresolved record discrepancies, requests outside volunteer authority, or disagreement continuing after clarification. The handoff includes both accounts, checked booking details, and the remaining question. Explain the next update route and use the stated fallback if staff cannot respond.

Needs: one facilitator, triads, coordinated cards, fictional records, and an explicit authority excerpt. No personal disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice. Identity invariance applies only when the changed detail is irrelevant under policy; legitimate accommodation rules must not be treated as bias.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator owns a first trial comparing this session with equal-length pause-and-replay training. Randomly distribute unseen assessment versions with identical evidence but exchanged claimant presentation; each trainee answers only one version individually. Check listening, verification, supported action, and differences between versions. Track an added risk: ignoring a detail that the policy explicitly makes relevant. Stop the swap exercise if that error appears, or if allocation differences and premature siding do not improve enough to justify preparing paired cards. Small samples offer a usability signal, not a reliable estimate of bias reduction.

EXPAND.title: Close the loop before implementing a decision
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: give both room users a structured opportunity to correct the volunteer’s understanding before the volunteer implements a next step. Then check that both understand what happens next. This creates an error-detection channel: a misheard claim or misunderstood handoff can be repaired while the interaction is still recoverable. Agreement with the outcome is not required.

Preparation: role cards include an ordinary detail that is easy to confuse, such as adjacent time slots or similarly named rooms. Users correct inaccurate summaries when invited. Records and policy supply enough information for a routine resolution in some rounds and require staff assistance in another. Avoid hidden passwords or trick disclosures.

Run 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 5–10 the facilitator models a brief correction exchange; 10–28 run three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 28–34 review corrections and repeat unclear closing explanations; 34–43 assess an unseen case individually; 43–45 review escalation and follow-up.

The volunteer listens to both parties, checks room/date/time/status, then says, ‘Here is what I understand each of you is reporting, and here is what the record shows. What have I misunderstood?’ After correcting errors and rechecking material discrepancies, the volunteer explains an authorized action or handoff. Ask each party to state their understanding of the next step; clarify without demanding agreement.

Escalation check: use the excerpt’s safety route for immediate safety concerns; seek designated staff when records remain inconsistent, the action exceeds volunteer authority, or disagreement persists after clarification. Send both accounts, verified facts, corrections, and the outstanding decision. Explain who will update users and the fallback if staff are unavailable. A claimant’s refusal to confirm does not establish booking rights.

Needs: one facilitator, triads, cards, records, and an excerpt defining authority and contacts. Use only fictional conflicts, with no legal or disciplinary advice. Correction invitations may lengthen interactions and cannot resolve unreliable records.
EXPAND.experiment: The facilitator owns a first trial comparing this session with an equal-length three-gate session. The unseen individual assessment presents both accounts and a record, then supplies a scripted user correction and asks for the trainee’s revised action and closing explanation. Score whether material corrections trigger rechecking, both accounts remain represented, and escalation is justified. Track time and whether trainees mistake disagreement for a veto over a valid booking. Stop adding the correction loop if it produces that veto error or adds time without improving correction uptake or next-step clarity. Written performance leaves live delivery uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Calibrate authority and complete the staff handoff
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Calibrate the boundary between acting and handing off.” This is the primary source because it directly teaches the required act-versus-escalate decision with closely matched cases. Preserve its contrast exercise, both-party listening, record verification, routine actions, and policy fallback. Change one consequential step: requesting staff assistance does not complete the handoff.

Mechanism: contrast cases to locate the authority boundary, then rehearse responsibility until staff accept the request. The volunteer explicitly requests acceptance, tells users what remains pending, and follows the excerpt’s contact fallback if interrupted or unanswered. Before acceptance, the volunteer remains responsible for communicating the pending status within their role; this confers no authority to allocate a disputed booking. After acceptance, identify who will provide the next update. If interrupted, resume by rechecking the current record and pending request before acting.

Run 45 minutes with one facilitator: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and model listening; 6–12 compare a clear booking correction with conflicting current confirmations; 12–30 conduct three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and two claimants; 30–34 replay a failed handoff; 34–43 assess unseen cases individually; 43–45 review the escalation check. Every role-play includes both accounts, neutral summaries, and verification of room, date, time, and status. One claimant card introduces an unanswered staff request or interruption.

Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; insufficient or contradictory records, an exception beyond volunteer authority, or persistent disagreement after clarification—contact designated staff. Otherwise perform the authorized routine action. Handoff: both accounts, verified facts, unresolved decision, requested help, acceptance, and update responsibility. If contact fails, use the excerpt’s fallback without promising room allocation.

The facilitator prepares role cards, records, and an excerpt specifying authority, contacts, and an unavailable-staff fallback. If the excerpt omits that fallback, identify the missing instruction and leave allocation unresolved for staff; do not invent a waiting or room-use rule. Use fictional conflicts only, with no personal disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice. The added acceptance check costs a short exchange and cannot guarantee staff availability.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: the facilitator. First trial: run this session with one small cohort and the source session with another, using the same unseen individual assessment. Include a close pair requiring routine action versus staff assistance, plus an unfamiliar case involving an interruption before staff acceptance. Score listening to both parties, record verification, justified action or escalation, and correct responsibility while the request is pending. Also compare unnecessary referrals and time spent completing handoffs. Stop using the added procedure if trainees interpret pending responsibility as permission to decide the dispute, or if it adds delay without reducing abandoned requests. A small trial supports revision, not a claim of durable superiority.

EXPAND.title: Make evidence-gap practice recover when records cannot be trusted
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “An evidence-gap role-play.” This is the competitive second source because incomplete information gives listening and verification an immediate practical purpose. Preserve distributed claimant information, reasonable questions, evidence reveals, and cases with unresolved discrepancies. Change the record-use decision: trainees must distinguish reading an entry from establishing that it is the applicable current entry.

Mechanism: obtaining information from both claimants remains necessary, but the volunteer must stop treating a record as decisive when its own supplied fields show it may be stale or inapplicable. Prepare fictional records with explicit room, date, time, status, and update information. Include one clearly superseded printout alongside an identifiable current record, and another case where currency cannot be established. Do not use obscure metadata or hidden clues.

Run 45 minutes: 0–5 introduce policy and boundaries; 5–9 demonstrate checking whether an entry applies; 9–27 conduct three six-minute triad rounds with rotating volunteers; 27–34 reveal evidence and replay one unsupported decision; 34–42 assess unseen cases individually; 42–45 rehearse escalation. Each volunteer hears and summarizes both accounts, checks the booking details, establishes which supplied record is current when possible, and explains the authorized action. A newer-looking document is insufficient unless the fictional materials establish its status.

Escalation check: follow the policy’s safety route for immediate safety concerns. Escalate when applicable current status cannot be established, current evidence conflicts, authority is insufficient, or disagreement persists after clarification. Give staff both accounts, checked details, the specific uncertainty, and the requested decision. Until staff accept, communicate that the decision remains pending; use the excerpt’s unavailable-staff fallback. If new information arrives during the handoff, update the request before implementing an action.

Owner and needs: one facilitator prepares coordinated cards, records, and a policy excerpt defining authoritative records, volunteer actions, and contact routes. If the excerpt does not establish which record governs, the correct outcome is staff clarification. All situations are fictional; request no personal conflict accounts and provide no legal or disciplinary advice. This adds a bounded record check, but may encourage excessive doubt unless clear routine cases remain in practice.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: the facilitator. Compare the revised session with the source’s evidence-gap session in two small cohorts. Give each trainee an unseen individual close pair: one has a clearly authoritative current booking and permits routine action; the other differs only in unresolved record currency and requires escalation. Add an unfamiliar exception request with a valid current booking. Score both-party listening, booking checks, supported action, and justified escalation. Compare incorrect reliance on stale records, unnecessary referrals, and completion time. Stop or simplify the added check if trainees routinely reject explicitly authoritative records or spend time inspecting irrelevant details without reducing unsupported allocation. No improvement is assumed in advance.

EXPAND.title: State the decision criterion before hearing competing claims
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: prospective commitment to a policy-based criterion. Instead of relying on volunteers to notice premature siding afterward, have them state what evidence will govern before learning which claimant it favors. This changes the timing of the decision standard; it does not require the volunteer to decide early or secure claimant agreement.

At the opening contact, the volunteer says, for example: “I’ll hear each account and check the room, date, time, and current booking status. I can take the actions this policy allows; unresolved conflicts or exceptions go to staff.” The criterion comes from the supplied excerpt. After hearing both parties and checking the record, the volunteer explicitly connects the next action to that criterion. If a newly disclosed fact activates another policy provision, identify the provision and revise the criterion openly. Commitment must never override relevant evidence or policy.

Run 45 minutes with one facilitator: 0–6 introduce the fictional policy and boundaries; 6–11 model a criterion, both-party listening, verification, and a justified revision; 11–29 run three six-minute triad role-plays, rotating volunteer and claimants; 29–34 discuss whether decisions followed the announced criteria; 34–43 assess unseen cases individually; 43–45 review escalation. Role cards include a confident claimant pressing for an immediate answer, a clear booking correction, and a policy-relevant exception. Every round requires listening to both parties and inspecting the fictional booking record.

Escalation check: immediate safety concern—use the excerpt’s safety route; unresolved record conflict, missing authority, or continuing disagreement after clarification—seek designated staff. Carry both accounts, verified facts, the relevant policy criterion, and the unresolved decision into the handoff. Before staff acceptance, keep users informed of pending status; if contact is interrupted or unanswered, use the excerpt’s fallback and recheck the record before resuming.

Needs: printed role cards, fictional records, and an excerpt sufficiently clear to supply a decision criterion, authority limits, and contact fallback. The facilitator owns preparation. If the excerpt cannot support a criterion, the volunteer states the uncertainty and seeks staff clarification. Use no personal conflict disclosures or legal or disciplinary advice. The potential benefit is resistance to pressure-driven changes in standards; the risks are a scripted opening and rigidity when relevant new facts emerge.
EXPAND.experiment: Owner: the facilitator. In a bounded first trial, compare this session with a simple hear-both/check-record session of equal length. Individually assess an unseen close pair on opposite sides of the routine-action versus escalation boundary, plus an unfamiliar case where a newly revealed policy provision requires revising the initial criterion. Ask for the opening response, summaries of both accounts, record checks, final action, and any handoff. Compare premature siding, justified decisions, and inappropriate refusal to revise; also record response length as a burden measure. Stop the commitment exercise if trainees retain an invalid criterion after relevant evidence appears, or if it adds substantial scripting without reducing unsupported decisions. Written results leave live transfer uncertain.
